sections.text: Build recurring payments on Solana with Mesub: publish a plan, check a customer's access from your server, and let them subscribe and manage from your pages.

sections.heading: Recurring payments on Solana, billed from your server
sections.text:
Mesub charges a customer's wallet on a schedule, without holding their funds. The customer approves a plan once, Mesub pulls the price to your wallet at every period, and your server asks Mesub who has access.
You publish a plan in the dashboard, add `@mesub/node` to your server, and gate what is paid. A React widget is there for the wallet part if you want it.

sections.heading: Start here
sections.text:
Your first subscriber:
A plan, an API key, the server routes and a button, in four steps.
Check access:
Ask whether a customer has access, with `hasAccess`, a guard, or `GET /v1/access`.
Webhooks:
Hear when a subscription renews, misses a payment or ends.
API reference:
Every route with its parameters, its answers and its error codes. Try a request from the page.

sections.heading: Try it
sections.text:
Sign in to your own site and click the button. The window shows the plan, asks for a wallet, then for two approvals: the terms, then the first payment. Once it lands, `/api/analytics` answers for that customer.
The subscription appears in the dashboard under Subscriptions, with its first payment under Collection. From here Mesub charges it every period without anything more from you.
Next: check access in detail, and webhooks to be told when a subscription renews, misses a payment or ends.

What happens when a customer subscribes, how each period is charged, and where your server fits. Built on the Solana Foundation's subscriptions program.
A customer approves a plan once. After that, Mesub pulls the plan's price from their wallet to yours at every period, and your server asks Mesub whether a given customer has access.

sections.heading: The flow
sections.text: Your pages never call Mesub and never hold a key. The wallet signs in the browser, and everything else goes through your server.

sections.heading: What runs where
sections.text:
Where | What it does | What it holds
Your pages | Ask the wallet for its two signatures | Nothing secret
Your server | Creates subscriptions, checks access, receives webhooks | The API key
Mesub | Sends each charge, retries a missed one, records attempts | No funds
Solana | Holds the plan's terms and moves the tokens | The customer's delegation
Your customer has no Mesub account. Mesub finds them by the id you give them (`external_id`), by the wallet that pays, or by their email.

sections.heading: On chain
sections.text:
Mesub does not hold or route the money. Plans and subscriptions are accounts of the subscriptions program published by the Solana Foundation, open source (MIT) and audited by Cantina. Its address is `De1egAFMkMWZSN5rYXRj9CAdheBamobVNubTsi9avR44`.
Three accounts are involved, all PDAs of that program:
Account | One per | What it holds
`Plan` | plan, created by you | The price, the period, who receives
`SubscriptionAuthority` | wallet and token, the customer's | The right to move that token
`SubscriptionDelegation` | wallet and plan, the customer's | The terms signed and the period state

sections.heading: The plan
sections.text: Creating a plan in the dashboard sends one transaction, signed by your wallet, that creates the `Plan` account with its `mint`, `amount`, `period_hours` and `end_ts`. `amount` and `period_hours` are immutable. `destinations` lists the wallets that may receive the money, and `pullers` lists who may trigger a charge besides you: Mesub's puller is one of them, which is what lets Mesub charge on schedule without your signature. If you take it off the plan, charges are blocked until it is back, and your subscribers are not held to be late for it.

sections.heading: An end date
sections.text:
A plan runs until you close it, unless you give it an end date when you create it: the last day it charges, in UTC. It is written on chain as `end_ts`.
Rule | What it is
At the earliest | One billing period from now, plus five minutes
At the latest | 100 years from now
Once created | The date cannot be removed or pushed later
A date too close is refused with `end_date_too_soon`, and one too far with `end_date_too_far`. A plan left unsigned until its date is too close is refused with `end_date_stale`: change the date, then sign.
For your subscribers, the end date is where everything stops:
- Nobody has access past it, whatever period they paid for.
- The last period is charged in full, even when the plan ends inside it.
- Nothing is charged after it, and every subscription still running ends with `plan_ended`.
- Nobody can subscribe from then on.
The terms a customer signs name the date and say the first two. See when the plan has an end date.

sections.heading: The subscription
sections.text:
Subscribing creates the customer's `SubscriptionAuthority` for that token if they have none, and a `SubscriptionDelegation` to your plan, which tracks `amount_pulled_in_period`, `current_period_start_ts` and `expires_at_ts`. The authority is approved as delegate on their token account; it can only move tokens when a delegation says so, and a delegation only allows this:
- up to the plan's `amount` per period, counted in `amount_pulled_in_period`,
- to one of the plan's `destinations`,
- triggered by the plan's owner or one of its `pullers`,
- while `expires_at_ts` is zero or in the future.
The delegation copies the plan's terms when it is created, so a customer keeps the price they signed for.
Both accounts cost rent, about 0.0036 SOL together. The customer pays it and gets it back when the subscription is closed.

sections.heading: A charge
sections.text: Each period, Mesub's puller sends a transfer instruction. The program checks the four conditions above, moves the tokens from the customer's token account to your destination, and updates the delegation's period counters. If the wallet is short, nothing moves and Mesub retries according to the plan's retry policy.

sections.heading: Cancelling
sections.text: Cancelling sets `expires_at_ts` to the end of the period already paid: access runs until then, and no further charge can land. The customer signs it, through your site or directly against the program. Resuming before that date clears it. Closing the delegation afterwards returns its rent.

sections.heading: Why your server asks Mesub and not the chain
sections.text:
A delegation that reads active on chain is not proof that the next charge will land: the wallet may be empty, or the customer may have revoked the token approval outside the program. Mesub tracks every attempt and its outcome, and `hasAccess` answers from that record, not from the account alone.
Next: your first subscriber, with a plan, an API key and the code. The SDKs are `@mesub/node` on the server and, optionally, `@mesub/react` in your pages.

Create a project's API key in the dashboard, put it on your server, check that it works, and rotate it when it leaks.
Every call your server makes to Mesub carries the project's API key. A project has one key at a time, and the key is the project: no call names a project id.

sections.heading: Create it
sections.text:
1. Open the dashboard and pick the project in the top bar.
2. Open Developers. Under API key, press Create the key.
3. Copy the key. It starts with `SUB_`.
The key is shown once. Mesub stores a hash of it, so nobody can read it again afterwards, you included. Once the window is closed, the dashboard only says that the project has a key and when it was last used. If you lose it, rotate it.

sections.heading: Put it on your server
sections.text:
```bash
MESUB_API_KEY=SUB_...
```
`@mesub/node` reads that variable by itself:
```ts
import { Mesub } from '@mesub/node';

const mesub = new Mesub(); // reads MESUB_API_KEY
```
Keep the key on your server. It creates subscriptions and reads your subscribers, so it never goes in a browser, a mobile app or a repository. The React widget does not need it: it talks to the routes `@mesub/node` mounts on your server.

sections.heading: Check that it works
sections.text:
```bash
curl "https://api.mesub.io/v1/project" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MESUB_API_KEY"
```
A `200` with the project's id means the key is good:
```json
{ "id": "cmufsl77w001ag2s6pp1ngf9p" }
```
In Developers, the line under the key then says it was last used just now.
Status | Code | Meaning
401 | `missing_api_key` | No `Authorization: Bearer` header was sent
401 | `invalid_api_key` | Not a key Mesub issued, or one rotated since

sections.heading: Rotate it
sections.text:
In Developers, Rotate draws a new key and shows it once, like the first.
The old key stops working at that moment. There is no period where both are accepted, so rotate when you are ready to deploy the new one: between the rotation and your deploy, your server's calls answer `401`.
Rotate when a key may have leaked, when someone who knew it leaves, or when it is lost.
Next: your first subscriber, or the API reference.

Ask Mesub whether a customer has access before serving a paid route, with hasAccess, a guard, or GET /v1/access. What the answer says and what happens during an outage.
Your own login says who the user is. Mesub says whether they have access to a plan. Ask before serving anything paid.

sections.heading: Ask the question
Who to ask about
sections.text:
Name the customer by exactly one of these:
By | Use it when | Good to know
`external_id` | Your app has its own login | Follows the person whichever wallet pays
`wallet` | The connected wallet is the customer | A string alone works too
`email` | A support lookup | The address they typed when subscribing, never verified by Mesub
`external_id` is the id you passed when the subscription was created. The widget routes pass it for you, from what your `customer` function returns.

sections.heading: Read the answer
sections.text:
`hasAccess` keeps only `access`. To show a customer where they stand, `access` returns the whole answer:
```ts
const answer = await mesub.access({ external_id: user.id }, 'pro');
```
See a full answer:
```json
{
    "wallet": "9xQeWvG816bUx9EPjHmaT23yvVM2ZWbrrpZb9PusVFin",
    "plan": "pro",
    "subscription_id": "cmg1x0abc0001",
    "access": true,
    "status": "active",
    "paused": false,
    "end_reason": null,
    "late_reason": null,
    "stop_reason": null,
    "payment_status": "paid",
    "blocked_since": null,
    "blocked_reason": null,
    "subscribed_since": "2026-01-01T00:00:05.000Z",
    "first_subscribed_at": "2026-01-01T00:00:05.000Z",
    "current_period_end": "2026-01-31T00:00:00.000Z",
    "cancelled_at": null,
    "access_until": "2026-01-31T00:00:00.000Z",
    "closable": false,
    "closable_from": null,
    "next_charge_at": "2026-01-31T00:00:00.000Z",
    "next_retry_at": null,
    "retry_deadline": null,
    "revalidate_after": 300
}
```
Field | What it says
`access` | The only field a guard needs. False from the plan's end date on
`status` | Where the subscription stands: `none`, `pending`, `active`, `unpaid`, `cancelled`, `stopped`, `ended`, `failed`, `superseded`
`payment_status` | `paid`, `late` or `none`
`subscription_id` | The subscription the answer is about, to cancel, resume, close or retry it without listing first. Null with `status` `none`
`late_reason` | Why an `unpaid` one is late, or why a `stopped` one stopped paying: see late payments. Null otherwise
`stop_reason` | Why a `stopped` one stopped: see late payments. Null otherwise
`blocked_since` | Since when its charges are held for a reason that is not the customer's. Null otherwise
`blocked_reason` | Why they are held: see blocked charges. Null otherwise
`access_until` | When access ends unless a charge renews it, never later than the plan's end date. Null while `access` is false
`next_charge_at` | The next charge. Null when a retry is pending instead, or when the plan ends before it
`next_retry_at` | The next retry of a missed charge. Null when the plan ends before it
`closable` | Whether the customer can close it now and get its deposit back, as Mesub last read the chain
`closable_from` | When it can be closed, if not now. Null when `closable` is true, or when no date is known yet
`wallet` | The wallet that pays. Null when the customer has nothing on that plan
`revalidate_after` | Seconds this answer stays true. The SDK caches it for that long
Read `access` to decide, never `status`. On a plan with an end date, nobody has access past that date, and for a few minutes after it `status` can still read `active` or `unpaid` with `access: false`.
When charges are blocked, the status does not change and the answer says since when, why, and when access ends. Here Mesub's puller was taken off a monthly plan that keeps the default retries:
```json
{
    "access": true,
    "status": "active",
    "payment_status": "paid",
    "blocked_since": "2026-01-31T00:02:00.000Z",
    "blocked_reason": "puller_not_allowed",
    "current_period_end": "2026-01-31T00:00:00.000Z",
    "access_until": "2026-02-03T00:06:00.000Z"
}
```
Mesub may add a status later, so keep a default branch. Asked with `{ attempts: true }`, the answer also carries the last charges. Read an attempt explains their `outcome` and `reason`.
Without a plan, `accessList` answers every plan the customer has anything on:
```ts
const { plans } = await mesub.accessList({ external_id: user.id });
```

sections.heading: What a guard answers
sections.text:
Status | When | Body
401 | `customer` returned nothing: nobody is signed in | `{ access: false, reason: 'unauthenticated' }`
402 | Mesub said this customer has no access | `{ access: false, reason: 'no_access', status }`
503 | Mesub could not answer about a customer it never saw | `{ access: false, reason: 'unavailable' }`
A 402 only ever means Mesub said no. To answer differently, a redirect to your pricing page for instance, pass `onDenied`.

sections.heading: Errors
When Mesub does not answer
sections.text:
The SDK caches each answer for its `revalidate_after`. If Mesub then fails, is too slow, or answers that the rate limit is reached:
- `hasAccess` and the guards serve the last answer they knew for that customer and plan, for up to 24 hours. A paying customer is not locked out by an outage.
- For a customer never seen before, `hasAccess` answers `false` and a guard answers 503 with the `Retry-After` Mesub sent, or 30 seconds when it sent none.
- `access` throws instead, since it is meant for a screen.
A guard never waits on Mesub more than 2 seconds for this check (`guardTimeout`).

Every status a Mesub subscription goes through, what each grants, how a missed payment is retried, and what cancelling, resuming and ending do.
A subscription has one `status` at a time. It is what `GET /v1/access` and every webhook carry.

sections.heading: Statuses
sections.text:
`status` | `access` | `payment_status` | What it means
`none` | false | `none` | This customer never subscribed to this plan. Not an error
`pending` | false | `none` | Reserved, waiting for the wallet's transaction to land
`active` | true | `paid` | Paid up. The next charge is at `next_charge_at`
`unpaid` | true, false on Free | `late` | A charge missed. A retry is coming
`cancelled` | true until the end | `paid` | The customer cancelled. The period already paid runs to `access_until`
`stopped` | false | `none` | Charging stopped, most often when the retries ran out. `stop_reason` says why
`ended` | false | `none` | Over. `end_reason` says why
`failed` | false | `none` | What landed on chain is not what Mesub reserved, so it is not billed. Rare
`superseded` | false | `none` | Replaced by a newer subscription of the same wallet to the same plan
`ended`, `failed` and `superseded` are final. `stopped` is not: Mesub charges nothing more, but the wallet's approval stays open on Solana until the customer cancels then closes it, and until then they can come back.
Gate on `access`, not on `status`: a `cancelled` subscription still grants access for a while, an `unpaid` one may or may not, and an `active` one has none once its plan has ended.
A checkout nobody signed turns `expired`. It never appears in `/v1/access`. It does in `GET /v1/subscriptions`, when you read a subscription by its id, and in the `subscription.expired` webhook. Only a `superseded` one is left out of the list.

sections.heading: Late payments
sections.text:
When a charge misses, most often because the wallet holds less than the price, the subscription turns `unpaid` and `payment_status` reads `late`.
`late_reason` says why, as the last failed charge found it. A `stopped` subscription keeps it too, for the payment it stopped on. It is null on every other status, and when Mesub cannot name the cause.
`late_reason` | What happened | What fixes it
`insufficient_balance` | The wallet holds less than the price | Adding funds
`approval_revoked` | The wallet no longer lets Mesub charge it | Not adding funds
`authority_closed` | The wallet closed its authorisation, for good | Nothing
An approval is revoked in the wallet itself, or replaced when another app is approved on the same token. Read `late_reason` before you tell a customer to top up. Every charge and retry is kept with its own outcome and reason: read an attempt says what each means.

sections.heading: On Dev and Business
sections.text:
Mesub retries on its own. A plan gets 3 retries by default, so a period has 4 tries in all. Each retry waits a quarter of the period, one day at most:
Plan period | Wait between tries
1 month | 1 day
1 week | 1 day
1 day | 6 hours
1 hour | 15 minutes
Access stays on while retries run. `next_retry_at` says when the next one is, `next_retry_number` and `retries_allowed` say which one it is, and `access_until` is the date of the last retry: if that one fails too, the subscription turns `stopped` and access ends.
A retry that pays turns it back to `active`. On `insufficient_balance` the customer has nothing to sign: they only need to add funds.
You can change the number of retries and the wait between them per plan, in the plan's Retry policy in the dashboard. All the retries must fit inside one period.

sections.heading: On Free
sections.text: There are no automatic retries, and an `unpaid` subscription grants no access. You can retry by hand, up to 3 times, until `retry_deadline`: from the dashboard, or from your own page with a retry. Past that date the subscription turns `stopped`.

sections.heading: Paying now
sections.text: On any tier, a late payment can be paid at once rather than at its next retry, for a customer who just topped up: from the dashboard, or from your server with `subscriptions.retry`, which the widget shows as Pay now. Pay a late payment now has the detail.

sections.heading: Why a subscription stops
sections.text:
A `stopped` subscription carries `stop_reason`. It is null on every other status, and on one that stopped before Mesub recorded why.
`stop_reason` | What happened | What the customer can do
`out_of_retries` | Every retry of the missed payment failed | Come back, or cancel then close
`retry_deadline_passed` | On Free, the last day to pay the missed payment passed | Come back, or cancel then close
`authority_closed` | The wallet closed its authorisation for good. Nobody can charge it | Close it at once (`closable` is true)
One stopped with `authority_closed` cannot come back: the customer closes it, then subscribes anew.

sections.heading: Blocked charges
sections.text:
A charge can also fail for a reason that is not the customer's. The subscription is then blocked: its charges are held, and the customer is never counted late for it.
The status does not change. A blocked subscription stays `active`, or `unpaid` if it was late already, and `payment_status` stays as it was. Two fields say it instead, on `GET /v1/access` and on the subscription: `blocked_since`, the date the block began, and `blocked_reason`. Both are null on a subscription that is not blocked.
`blocked_reason` | What happened | What it asks of you
`puller_not_allowed` | Mesub's puller was taken off the plan on chain | Add Mesub back to the plan's pullers, with the wallet that owns the plan
`receiver_not_allowed` | The receiving wallet is not among the plan's destinations | Choose a receiving wallet that is among them
`receiver_account_missing` | It has no account for the plan's token, and nobody else can be paid | Open an account for that token
`receiver_account_frozen` | The token account it is paid into is frozen | Have it thawed, or choose another receiving wallet
`mint_gone` | The plan's token no longer exists | Create a new plan with another token
`mesub` | Any cause on Mesub's side | Nothing
The first five are your plan's own setup, and only you can undo them. `mesub` covers every other cause, whatever it is.
Mesub keeps trying: about every ten minutes, then less often, at least once a day, once a subscription blocked by the plan's setup has lost its access. `next_charge_at` is the next try, or `next_retry_at` on a subscription that was late already. The first charge that goes through, or that the chain holds as paid, lifts the block. Access comes back with it, and the customer has nothing to sign.
Access has an end all the same, and `access_until` is its date:
`blocked_reason` | Access lasts
`mesub` | To the end of the period after the one paid for
One of your setup | Past the paid period, as long as the plan's retries give a late payment
It is never less than a few minutes after the end of the paid period, which is what a plan with no retry, and any plan on Free, gets. It is never later than the end of the period after the one paid for. `access` is never true past `access_until` on a blocked subscription.
`blocked_since` is the date of the block `blocked_reason` names: when a cause on Mesub's side gives way to one of your setup, or back, it starts again.

sections.heading: Cancelling and resuming
sections.text:
The customer cancels by signing one transaction with the wallet that pays. It moves no money: it records on chain that the subscription ends with the period already paid.
Field | Before | After cancelling
`status` | `active` | `cancelled`
`access` | true | true until `access_until`
`cancelled_at` | null | When they cancelled
`next_charge_at` | a date | null
Until `access_until`, they can resume: one more signature, and the subscription is `active` again with its next charge back on schedule.
After `access_until`, it turns `ended` with `end_reason: "cancelled"`. The customer can then close it to get the rent of its account back.

sections.heading: When the plan has an end date
sections.text:
A plan can carry an end date, set when you create it. `ends_at` on the plan says when, and is null on a plan with no end.
Access stops at the plan's end for everybody. `access` is false from that moment on, for a subscription that is `active`, `unpaid`, `cancelled` or parked alike, and `access_until` is never later than the plan's end.
The last period is charged in full, even when the plan ends inside it. Mesub does not prorate it, and paying it does not carry access past the plan's end. The terms the customer signs when subscribing say both.
Once the plan ends before the next charge, nothing more is charged, and the dates say so:
Field | What it reads near the plan's end
`access_until` | The plan's end, when the paid period or the retries run past it
`next_charge_at` | null: a subscription in its last period has no next charge
`next_retry_at` | null when the plan ends before the retry
`retry_deadline` | On Free, the plan's end when it comes before the deadline
At the plan's end, a subscription that is `active` or `unpaid` turns `ended` with `end_reason: "plan_ended"`, and `subscription.ended` is sent. One the customer had cancelled ends with `cancelled`, as it would have.
Mesub ends it within a few minutes of the plan's end. For that long `status` can still read `active` or `unpaid` while `access` is already false. It never reads `ended` with `access` true. A guard reads `access`, never `status`.
From its end on, a plan takes no new subscriber either: creating a subscription to it is refused with `plan_ended`.

sections.heading: Why a subscription ends
sections.text:
An `ended` subscription carries one `end_reason`:
`end_reason` | What happened
`cancelled` | The customer cancelled and the paid period ran out
`plan_ended` | The plan reached its own end date
`plan_removed` | You deleted the plan
`plan_replaced` | Another plan now stands at its address
`closed_elsewhere` | It was closed on chain, outside Mesub
`closed` | The customer closed the subscription through Mesub
It is null on every other status.

sections.heading: Parked seats
sections.text: A project holds a limited number of subscribers on Free and Dev. After a downgrade, the seats over the limit are parked: `paused` is true, the `status` stays as it was, nothing is charged, and access runs to the end of the period already paid. Moving back up a tier puts them back on schedule.

sections.heading: Coming back
sections.text:
A customer whose subscription stopped or ended can subscribe again to the same plan, with the same wallet. The new subscription takes over. A `stopped` one turns `superseded`; an `ended` one stays as it was. A stopped subscription holds no seat, so coming back needs a free one, like any new subscriber: on a full project it is refused with `seat_cap_reached`.
A return asked within about two minutes of the end of the old subscription's billing period is refused with `comeback_period_rolling`, so the terms the wallet signs name the period that is really charged. Wait for the `Retry-After` it carries, then create the subscription again: a transaction built before the wait is not sent.
`subscribed_since` is the start of the current one, and `first_subscribed_at` the start of the very first.

Register an endpoint, verify each delivery with its signing secret, and react to renewals, missed payments and cancellations.
`hasAccess` is enough to gate a route. Webhooks are for reacting when something changes: a renewal, a missed payment, a cancellation.

sections.heading: Set up your endpoint
sections.text:
In the dashboard, open Developers, then Webhooks, add your URL and pick its events. Put the endpoint's signing secret in your server's environment:
```bash
MESUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET=whsec_...
```
An endpoint must be a public HTTPS URL. A project can have up to 16.

sections.heading: Rotate the secret
sections.text:
Regenerate the secret on the endpoint's page in the dashboard, with an overlap of up to 24 hours. The old secret keeps signing beside the new one until the overlap ends: each delivery in that window carries two signatures in `webhook-signature`, the new secret's first, and `verify` accepts it when any one matches. So nothing changes on your side until you deploy the new secret as `MESUB_WEBHOOK_SECRET`, and nothing fails if you deploy it before the overlap ends.
With no overlap, the old secret stops at once: every delivery fails verification until the new one is deployed. Use no overlap when the old secret leaked. Rotating again during an overlap ends the oldest secret.

sections.heading: Create a handler
See a delivery before writing any code
sections.text:
webhook.site gives you a public URL that shows every request it receives. It is the quickest way to see what Mesub sends.
1. Open webhook.site and copy Your unique URL.
2. In the dashboard, under Developers then Webhooks, add that URL as an endpoint.
3. On that endpoint, click Send test.
4. Back on webhook.site, the request appears with its JSON body and three headers: `webhook-id`, `webhook-timestamp` and `webhook-signature`.
The signing secret is not in the request. It stays in the dashboard, and your handler uses it to check `webhook-signature`. Remove the endpoint when you are done: it would receive your real events too.

sections.heading: Send a test event to your own handler
sections.text:
In the dashboard, on your endpoint, pick the event to simulate and click Send test. With no event picked, the plain `test` event is sent. A test delivery is signed like a real one and carries `"test": true` at the top of its body, with a made-up subscription whose id is `sub_test`, so your handler can recognise and ignore it.
The endpoint must be enabled, and one test is pending at a time: wait for it to be delivered before sending the next.
A handler running on your machine needs a public URL. A tunnel such as ngrok gives it one.

sections.heading: Events
sections.text:
Event | Sent when
`subscription.created` | The first payment landed
`subscription.renewal_upcoming` | A renewal is near, and whether it can pay
`subscription.renewed` | A period was paid
`subscription.payment_failed` | A charge missed
`subscription.stopped` | Mesub stopped charging after missed payments
`subscription.cancelled` | The customer cancelled; access runs to the period's end
`subscription.resumed` | A cancellation was undone
`subscription.ended` | It is over; `data.end_reason` says why. At a cancellation's end, not sent yet
`subscription.expired` | A checkout was started and never signed
`subscription.paused` | A seat was parked over the tier's limit. Not sent yet
`subscription.unpaused` | A parked seat is back. Not sent yet
`subscription.access_granted` | Access started, and was off just before. Not sent yet
`subscription.access_revoked` | Access ended, and was on just before. Not sent yet
`test` | You sent one from the dashboard
"Not sent yet" means Mesub writes none of these today, whatever the reference page of the event says: they come on together, later. A cancellation's end still reads `ended` on the subscription, and closing it sends `subscription.ended` today.
Mesub may add a type later: keep a default branch. The reference has one page per event, with its payload.

sections.heading: The event object

Every event has the same shape: its `id`, its `type`, when Mesub wrote it (`created_at`), its `sequence` among the subscription's events, `data`, the subscription as `subscriptions.retrieve` answers it, and `detail`, which is the event's own. `event.id` is the same in every delivery of the event: apply each event once by it. sections.heading: Drive access from the access events
The first payment
Cancellations that end, parked seats
sections.text:
Three transitions get their own event once Mesub turns them on, with the access events:
- A cancellation reaches its expiry. `subscription.access_revoked` is sent at the expiry itself. `subscription.ended`, with `end_reason: "cancelled"`, follows once Mesub has read the chain, usually within half an hour, with `detail.changed_at` at the expiry. Closing the subscription later sends `subscription.ended` again, with `end_reason: "closed"`: that one is sent today.
- A seat is parked over the project's tier limit: `subscription.paused`. It is not a pause the customer asked for. The status stays as it was, `data.paused` is true, and access runs to the end of the period paid for.
- A parked seat is brought back: `subscription.unpaused`, `data.paused` false. Mesub charges it again.
A parked seat's access change still comes as `access_revoked` or `access_granted`, with a higher `sequence`: see parked seats.

sections.heading: Before a renewal
sections.text:
`subscription.renewal_upcoming` is sent once per period, when a subscription enters the last quarter of it, and three days before the charge at most: three days ahead on a monthly plan, six hours on a daily one. Mesub reads the customer's wallet at that moment, and `detail` says what the coming charge would meet:
```json
{
    "can_pay": false,
    "renewal_issue": "balance",
    "amount": "9990000",
    "mint": "EPjFWdd5AufqSSqeM2qN1xzybapC8G4wEGGkZwyTDt1v",
    "due_at": "2026-03-02T00:00:00.000Z"
}
```
Field | What it holds
`can_pay` | Whether the charge would go through as the wallet stood when it was read
`renewal_issue` | `balance`, `authority`, or null when it can pay
`amount` | What will be charged, in the token's smallest unit
`mint` | The token
`due_at` | When the charge is due
`balance` means the wallet holds less than the amount, or has no account for the token: the customer adds funds. `authority` means Mesub can no longer move the tokens: the approval was replaced or is too small, or the account is frozen. Subscribing again gives a new approval.
It is sent whether the charge can pay or not, so it also works as a plain reminder before a renewal. It is a reading, not a promise: a wallet topped up or emptied afterwards changes the outcome, and the charge itself answers with `subscription.renewed` or `subscription.payment_failed`.
An endpoint receives it only if that event is selected for it in the dashboard: an endpoint created before it existed does not get it by itself. Mesub also mails the customer when the charge cannot pay and the subscription carries an email.
It is never sent for a charge that cannot happen. A subscription in the last period of a plan with an end date has no renewal: no event, and no mail.

sections.heading: At a plan's end
sections.text:
A plan can have an end date, and three events read differently around it.
Event | What changes
`subscription.renewal_upcoming` | Not sent in the last period: the plan ends before the next charge
`subscription.payment_failed` | Can carry `next_retry_at: null` and `retries_left: 0` in `detail`
`subscription.ended` | Sent at the plan's end, with `data.end_reason` at `plan_ended`
A charge that misses when the plan ends before the next retry has no retry to announce: `next_retry_at` is null, `retries_left` is 0 and `retry_mode` is null. The subscription stays `unpaid` until the plan's end, then ends. On Free, `retry_deadline` is the plan's end when that comes before the deadline.
`subscription.ended` arrives within a few minutes of the plan's end, for a subscription that was still `active` or `unpaid`. Access has stopped at the end itself: an event delivered in between can carry `status: "active"` with `access: false`.

sections.heading: Retries
sections.text:
If your endpoint does not answer with a 2xx, Mesub tries the same event again: after 1 minute, 5 minutes, 30 minutes, 2 hours, then every 12 hours, for about three days in all. Each retry carries the same `event.id` as the first try.
An endpoint that fails for three days with no success in between is disabled. Fix it, then enable it again in the dashboard.

sections.heading: Duplicates
sections.text: The same event can arrive more than once. Store the ids you handled and drop a repeat.

sections.heading: Order
sections.text: Order is not guaranteed: a retry can land after a later event. Each event carries `sequence`, its place among the subscription's events (1, 2, 3...): apply a subscription's events in that order and skip one lower than the last you applied. An event without `sequence` cannot be placed: ask `hasAccess`, or retrieve the subscription, rather than trust its `data`.

Add a subscribe button and a manage window to a React app with @mesub/react. It handles the wallet and calls your own server, never Mesub.
`@mesub/react` is the wallet part of subscribing, ready made: picking a wallet, connecting it, and signing in the right order. It is optional. Everything it does goes through routes on your own server, so it holds no key and never calls Mesub.
It is not a wallet connector for your site. It asks a wallet for an account when it needs a signature, and never disconnects one.

sections.heading: Set it up
Subscribe
Manage
Theming
When something goes wrong
sections.text:
Each case has its own screen, and says whether anything was charged.
What happens | What the widget does
Nobody is signed in on your site | Says to sign in first. Nothing to sign
No wallet is installed | Links to Phantom and Solflare
The wallet refuses | Nothing is submitted. Try again starts over
The terms expired before they were signed | Asks your server again and shows the review with fresh terms
The wrong wallet is used to manage | Says which wallet pays. Nothing is signed
Mesub refuses, for instance already subscribed | Shows Mesub's message as written
The network fails after the payment was sent | "Payment may be pending", and Check again, which never pays twice
Mesub is busy at submit (a 503 with a wait) | Mesub sent nothing: it waits, then sends the same request once more; still busy, it says how long to wait, with Check again
Mesub is busy at Pay now | Nothing was charged: the button counts down, about 20 seconds, then can be pressed again

sections.heading: Show the plan and its token
sections.text:
A pricing page of your own reads the plan on your server and shows what the customer will pay, and in which token.
```ts
const plan = await mesub.plans.retrieve('pro'); // or mesub.plans.list()
```
Field | What it says
`amount_display` | The price per period, as a person counts it: `9.99`
`amount_usd` | That price in US dollars, or null when it has no price
`symbol` | Set only for a token Mesub vouches for, null otherwise
`token.symbol` | The token's symbol, as Mesub found it, or null
`token.name` | The token's name, or null
`token.logo_url` | The token's logo, or null
`token.verified` | Whether the token is one a customer can take at its word
`mint` | The token's address, which is the token
Mesub fills `token` itself, from the plan's exact mint: nothing in it is typed by you or sent by the browser. `verified` is true for the tokens Mesub vouches for, USDC, USDT and PYUSD, and for one Jupiter marks as verified.
Show an unverified token as unverified, and keep its mint in view. A symbol is free text on chain: anyone can create a token and call it USDC, and a fake under a known name is a common scam. Mesub never answers an unverified token under the symbol or the name of a stablecoin it vouches for: that field is null. Any other symbol comes as the token wrote it, so the page says which kind it is:
```ts
import type { Plan } from '@mesub/node';

function tokenLabel(plan: Plan): string {
    const { symbol, verified } = plan.token;
    const mint = `${plan.mint.slice(0, 4)}...${plan.mint.slice(-4)}`;

    if (!symbol) return mint;
    return verified ? symbol : `${symbol}, unverified (${mint})`;
}
```
`amount_usd` is a decimal string, `"9.99"`. On a plan it is an estimate: the plan's amount at the latest price Mesub knows for the token, so it moves with the market for anything but a stablecoin. Show it as about that much, never as the price: the customer is charged `amount` of the token, whatever it is worth that day. It is null when Mesub has no price. What each charge was worth is on the attempt.
See these fields on a plan in another token:
```json
{
    "slug": "supporter",
    "name": "Supporter",
    "amount": "3000000000",
    "amount_display": "30000",
    "amount_usd": "0.45",
    "decimals": 5,
    "symbol": null,
    "mint": "DezXAZ8z7PnrnRJjz3wXBoRgixCa6xjnB7YaB1pPB263",
    "token": {
        "symbol": "Bonk",
        "name": "Bonk",
        "logo_url": "https://arweave.net/hQiPZOsRZXGXBJd_82PhVdlM...",
        "verified": true
    }
}
```

sections.heading: A plan with an end date
sections.text:
Nobody has access past a plan's end date, and the last period is charged in full even when the plan ends inside it. Mesub writes both in the terms, so the customer reads them before signing. These are the lines of `terms.message` that say what is charged, for a plan of 20 USDC every 30 days.
With no end date:
```text
Amount: 20 USDC every 30 days
First charge: 20 USDC now, in the transaction you sign next
Then: 20 USDC every 30 days, until you cancel
```
With an end date, two more lines:
```text
Amount: 20 USDC every 30 days
First charge: 20 USDC now, in the transaction you sign next
Then: 20 USDC every 30 days, until you cancel, or the plan ends on 2027-01-01
Last charge: 20 USDC, in full, for the last period that starts before the plan ends
Access: stops when the plan ends on 2027-01-01, even if the last period paid for is not over
```
When the plan ends before a second charge can be made, the first one is the only one:
```text
Amount: 20 USDC, a single charge
Single charge: 20 USDC now, in full, in the transaction you sign next
Access: until the plan ends on 2026-10-02, even if the period paid for is not over
No further charge: the plan ends on 2026-10-02
```
The date is the plan's end, as a day in UTC. Show the message as it is: a page that words these lines differently tells the customer something other than what they sign.
Terms that name a second charge are refused at `submit` with `terms_changed` if the plan's end has come too close for it meanwhile. Create again: the new terms say it is a single charge. Once the plan has ended, `create` is refused with `plan_ended`.

sections.heading: How long submit takes
sections.text:
`submit` waits for the chain, so it is slow by design: up to 90 seconds for one send, and up to 130 seconds in all with its own retries. That is longer than many serverless functions allow. Lower it there:
```ts
await mesub.subscriptions.submit(id, body, { timeout: 25_000, budget: 40_000 });
```
A retry sends the same request again. Mesub recognises what it already co-signed and answers from the chain, so a customer is never charged twice.
A 503 `unavailable` with a `Retry-After` means too many submits are waiting on your project, and Mesub signed and sent nothing. `submit` sends the same request again after the wait, and past its retries throws it, `retryable`, with `retryAfter`.

sections.heading: When the outcome is unknown
Refusals
sections.text:
Each one is thrown as a `MesubError`. `apiCode` says which:
On | `apiCode` | What to do
`create` | `already_subscribed` | This wallet already holds this plan
`create` | `insufficient_balance` | The wallet cannot pay the first period
`create` | `plan_not_found` | Fix the slug
`create` | `plan_ended` | The plan is past its end date
`submit` | `terms_expired` | Create again and sign the fresh terms
`submit` | `terms_changed` | The plan changed since. Create again
`submit` | `transaction_expired` | Ask for a new transaction and sign it
`submit` | `subscription_not_found` | The id is not one of your project's
`subscriptions.transaction` is refused like `create` when the plan or the wallet no longer allows the subscription, and with `not_awaiting_signature` when the subscription is no longer `pending`. Create again if it `expired`.
Calling `create` again for the same plan, wallet and customer, while nothing has landed, answers the same subscription with a fresh transaction. The customer is the `external_id` you gave, or the `email` when you gave no id. Another customer naming the same wallet gets a subscription of its own: only the one the wallet signs for lands, and the others on that wallet then read `expired`.

sections.heading: Read a subscription back

sections.text:
Let a customer cancel, resume or close a subscription from your own UI, and list its payments, with @mesub/node and no widget.
The React widget covers this with `ManageButton`. Without it, each action is two calls from your server with the wallet in between. The API key alone changes nothing: only the wallet that pays a subscription can sign.
To | Build | Confirm | It becomes
Stop the renewals of a running subscription | `cancel(id)` | `confirmCancel(id, { signature })` | `cancelled`
Take a cancellation back before its end | `resume(id)` | `confirmResume(id, { signature })` | `active`
Close one that is over, and return its rent | `close(id)` | `confirmClose(id, { signature })` | `ended`, `end_reason: "closed"`
Close takes a subscription that was cancelled or stopped and whose end has passed, one that ended with its plan, and at once one stopped with `stop_reason` `authority_closed`. `closable` and `closable_from`, on the subscription and on the access answer, say whether it can close now, and from when. One that ended with its plan keeps its `end_reason`, `plan_ended` for instance, once closed.

sections.heading: The three steps
What cancelling does
sections.text:
A cancellation is not an immediate stop. A subscription that is paid up keeps its access until the end of the period it paid for, and can be resumed until then. Once that date has passed it reads `ended`, and closing it returns the rent the wallet paid when subscribing.
A subscription cancelled while `unpaid` or `stopped` has no access, and its missed period is never collected.
On a plan with an end date, access never runs past the plan's end, cancelled or not. The last period is charged in full even when the plan ends inside it, and the terms the customer signed say so. Lifecycle has the detail.
Lifecycle has the detail.

sections.heading: Refusals
sections.text:
Each is thrown as a `MesubError`. `apiCode` says which:
`apiCode` | When
`subscription_not_found` | No subscription of your project under that id
`subscription_not_active` | `cancel`: it is not `active`, `unpaid` or `stopped`
`subscription_cancelled` | `cancel`: it was cancelled already
`subscription_not_cancelled` | `resume`: nothing cancelled it. `close`: it is neither cancelled nor stopped
`subscription_ended` | `resume`: the paid period is over. Subscribe again
`plan_removed` | `resume`: its plan is gone
`plan_replaced` | `resume`: another plan stands at its address
`close_too_early` | `close`: its end has not passed yet
`subscription_not_on_chain` | It is closed already
`nothing_to_confirm` | A confirm before any transaction was built
These six calls are limited to 60 a minute per API key. Each has its page in the reference, from cancel to confirm a close.

sections.heading: Pay a late payment now
sections.text:
A customer who topped up their wallet does not have to wait for the next retry. `retry` charges the missed period now, with nothing to sign: the wallet approved the plan when it subscribed.
```ts
const subscription = await mesub.subscriptions.retry(subscriptionId);
// still unpaid: the charge runs in the background
```
The answer is the subscription, still `unpaid`. The outcome comes as the `subscription.renewed` or `subscription.payment_failed` webhook, and on the subscription. The React widget shows it as Pay now, through `POST /subscriptions/:id/retry` of the routes, on a late subscription that can pay (`payable`), and `useSubscriptions` gives `payNow(id)` for a list of your own. `POST /v1/subscriptions/:id/retry` is the call without the SDK.
It is refused before anything is queued when it cannot succeed, as the chain reads now, so no retry is spent for nothing:
`apiCode` | When
`insufficient_balance` | The wallet holds less than the period costs. Top up first
`retry_cannot_succeed` | The wallet no longer approves it, its token account is frozen, or its authority is closed
`retry_too_soon` | The wait since the last try is not over. `retryAfter` says when
`subscription_not_late` | It is not `unpaid`
`subscription_paused` | Its seat is parked
`retries_spent` | On Free, the three retries of the period are spent
`retry_deadline_passed` | On Free, `retry_deadline` has passed
`plan_ended` | Its plan has ended
`subscription_changed` | Two retries met, or a charge moved it on. Retryable: read it back first
`pull_running` | On Free, a charge runs now. Retryable
A 503 changed nothing: `unavailable` when the charge could not be queued, or `network_unavailable`. `retryAfter` says when to ask again.
How often:
Tier | Retries by hand
Free | Three per missed period, whoever makes them, at least 10 minutes apart, none in the last 2 minutes of the missed period
Dev, Business | Beside the plan's own retries, uncounted. The first at once, then 20 minutes, 40, 80, doubling
The same retry is in the dashboard. `retry` is sent once, never retried by the SDK, and limited to 60 a minute per API key.

sections.heading: Read an attempt
sections.text:
An attempt is one try at charging one period. Mesub keeps every one, whatever came of it: the charge that paid, the one that failed, and the one it never sent.
`outcome` says how it ended:
`outcome` | What happened | Sent to the chain | Uses a retry
`paid` | The transfer landed: the period is paid | Yes | No
`skipped` | Mesub read the chain first and found nothing it could charge | No | No
`rejected` | The charge failed on the customer's side | No, or refused by the program | Yes
`blocked` | The charge could not be made, and the customer has no part in it | No, or not known yet | No
Only a `paid` attempt carries a `signature`, since only it moved money. A `rejected` one moved nothing: Mesub reads the wallet's balance before it sends, and a transfer the program refuses changes nothing. A `blocked` one mostly stopped before sending, and Mesub comes back to it ten minutes later. A block of your plan's own setup that has outlived the customer's access is tried less often: each wait as long as the block has lasted, up to a day, or a quarter of the period on a shorter plan. When a transfer did go out and Mesub could not see it land, it asks the chain before charging again, and records a `paid` attempt if it landed.
**Only `rejected` counts against the customer.** The one at the due date turns the subscription `unpaid`. Each retry rejected after it is one retry spent, and when the last is spent the subscription turns `stopped`. A `blocked` or `skipped` attempt never uses a retry, however many there are. Neither does a retry fired by hand on Dev or Business, from the dashboard or with `retry`: it is recorded like any other, and the plan's retries stay as they were.

sections.heading: Reasons
sections.text:
`reason` says why an attempt did not pay. It is null on a `paid` one, and a short stable string on every other.
What the customer did, or their wallet:
`reason` | `outcome` | What it says
`insufficient_balance` | `rejected` | The wallet holds less than the period owes, or has no token account
`token_account_reassigned` | `rejected` | The wallet's token account now belongs to someone else
`token_account_frozen` | `rejected` | The wallet's token account is frozen
`authority_closed` | `rejected` | The wallet is short, and its authorisation is closed for good
`program_1` | `rejected` | The wallet holds less than the period owes, or approved less
`program_4` | `rejected` | The wallet no longer lets Mesub charge it: the approval was revoked
`program_103`, `136` | `rejected` | The wallet closed its authorisation, or made a new one since
`program_508` | `rejected` | Cancelled on chain, and its expiry has passed
`cancelled` | `skipped` | Cancelled on chain, and the period already paid is over
`closed_elsewhere` | `skipped` | The subscription no longer exists on chain. It ends, `closed_elsewhere`
`program_103` and `program_136` count against the customer only once Mesub reads the authorisation and finds it closed. Then the subscription stops at once, `stop_reason` `authority_closed`, whatever the tier and the retries left. Until a read agrees, the attempt is `blocked`, and tried again.
`late_reason` reads four of these: `insufficient_balance`, `program_4` (`approval_revoked`), and `program_103`, `program_136` or `authority_closed` (`authority_closed`): see late payments.
What you did to the plan:
`reason` | `outcome` | What it says
`plan_removed` | `skipped` | The plan was deleted. The subscription ends, `plan_removed`
`plan_replaced` | `skipped` | Another plan stands at its address. It ends, `plan_replaced`
`plan_ended` | `skipped` | The plan's end date has passed. It ends, `plan_ended`
`receiver_not_allowed` | `blocked` | The plan's receiver is not among the destinations it allows
`receiver_account_missing` | `blocked` | Neither the receiver nor your wallet has an account for that token
`receiver_account_frozen` | `blocked` | The token account the plan pays is frozen
`puller_not_allowed` | `blocked` | Mesub's puller was taken off the plan
`program_130`, `501`, `506`, `516`, `519` | `blocked` | One of the changes above, made while the charge was on its way
What Mesub or the network did:
`reason` | `outcome` | What it says
`period_already_paid` | `skipped` | The chain holds the period as paid. Not a failure: `amount` is `0`
`period_missed` | `skipped` | A whole period went by before Mesub charged it. It is never collected
`terms_missing` | `blocked` | No terms were signed through Mesub. Never charged, and not tried again
`puller_missing` | `blocked` | Mesub's own record of the plan is incomplete
`mint_gone` | `blocked` | The token could not be read
`gone_unconfirmed` | `blocked` | The plan or the subscription read as gone once. Mesub reads it again
`send_unconfirmed` | `blocked` | A transfer is being sent, or its send was cut short
`landing_unknown` | `blocked` | An earlier transfer may have landed. Mesub waits for the chain to say
`program_400` | `blocked` | The program says the period is charged already: its clock is behind
`solana_<code>` | `blocked` | Any other error of the chain, with its number
`transport` | `blocked` | The network did not answer, or not in time
`program_<code>` comes under two outcomes: `rejected` for `1`, `4`, `103`, `136` and `508`, the codes that are the customer's doing, and `blocked` for every other code, those these tables name and any number nobody placed. This list can grow, and `<code>` is any number the chain answers, so keep a default branch on both `reason` and `outcome`.

sections.heading: The other fields
sections.text:
Field | What it says | Null when
`attempted_at` | When Mesub recorded the attempt | Never
`amount` | What was asked for, in the token's smallest unit, as a string | Never
`amount_usd` | `amount` in US dollars, at the token's price when it was charged | Not priced yet, or no price was found
`signature` | The transaction that paid | The outcome is not `paid`
`retry` | True when a charge for this period had already failed | Never
`retry_number` | Which retry it was. 1 is the first after the missed charge | It is not a retry
`retries_allowed` | How many retries the period had when the attempt ran | It is not a retry
`period_start` | The start of the period it was for | Mesub stopped before reading the period
`paid`, on the answer | `count` and `amount` of every `paid` attempt of the subscription | Never. `0` and `"0"` when none
`retry_number` and `retries_allowed` are kept as the attempt ran: changing the plan's retry policy later does not rewrite them. Both are also null, with `retry` true, on a retry fired by hand on Dev or Business, which is none of the plan's, and on the few attempts written while the subscription was changing under them. On Free every retry is fired by hand: those are the plan's, and carry both.
`period_start` is null on the reasons Mesub meets before it reads the period: `cancelled`, `closed_elsewhere`, the three `plan_` ones, `terms_missing`, `gone_unconfirmed` and `landing_unknown`, and on a `transport` or `solana_<code>` that failed on the very first read. On those, `amount` is the plan's price, where everywhere else it is what the period still owed. On a `paid` attempt it is what moved.
`amount_usd` is a decimal string, `"9.99"`. Unlike the plan's, it is not an estimate that moves: Mesub prices each attempt once, paid or not, at the instant of the charge, and never rewrites it. That takes a moment after the attempt is recorded, so read null as "not priced yet" and show the token amount alone until it comes. It stays null for a token no price was found for. A receipt shows `amount` in the token first: that is what moved. How to name the token is in Show the plan and its token.
The first attempt of a subscription is the payment the customer signed when subscribing, and its `signature` is that transaction.

Use the fake Mesub of @mesub/node/testing in your own tests: grant and deny access, simulate an outage, and send signed webhooks to your handler.
`@mesub/node/testing` is a fake Mesub for your own tests. It answers what the SDK asks from what each test sets, with no network and no Mesub account, and none of it ends up in your production bundle.
```ts
import { FakeMesub } from '@mesub/node/testing';

const fake = new FakeMesub();
const mesub = fake.client(); // a real Mesub client, wired to the fake
```
Call `fake.reset()` between tests, and take a new `fake.client()` in each one: `reset()` empties the fake, not the answers a client already cached, which it would serve again during a simulated outage. It also starts every id over (`sub_fake_1`, `evt_fake_1`, `msg_fake_1`, ...), so a test makes the same ids whatever ran before it.

sections.heading: Access
sections.text:
```ts
fake.grant({ external_id: 'user_42' }, 'pro'); // active and paid
fake.deny({ external_id: 'user_7' }, 'pro', { status: 'stopped' });

await mesub.hasAccess({ external_id: 'user_42' }, 'pro'); // true
await mesub.hasAccess({ external_id: 'user_7' }, 'pro'); // false
```
A customer is answered as named: a wallet you granted is not found by its `external_id`. For any other answer, `fake.setAccess(...)` takes the fields you want.
`new FakeMesub({ plans: ['pro'] })` makes every other slug answer `plan_not_found`, as a typo would. Name your plans this way to test the widget routes: they read the plan list, which is empty otherwise.
A plan that ends:
```ts
fake.grantLastPeriod({ external_id: 'user_7' }, 'pro', endsAt); // access until the plan ends
fake.endPlan('pro'); // the end passed: what is held on it ends with plan_ended
```

sections.heading: A guard, end to end
An outage
sections.text:
```ts
fake.fail('outage'); // every call answers 503, until fake.fail(null)
fake.fail({ status: 429, code: 'rate_limited', retryAfter: 2 });
fake.fail({ status: 503, code: 'unavailable' }); // Retry-After as Mesub: 2 s on submit, 20 s on retry
```
`fail()` answers every call, not only the one under test: a route that reads a subscription before it acts gets the error on that read.
This is how to check what your routes do when Mesub does not answer: a customer seen before keeps their last answer, one never seen gets a 503.
As on Mesub, a client keeps a yes up to five minutes and a no 10 seconds (the `revalidate_after` Mesub sends), so a change made after a client asked shows to a new `fake.client()`. `new FakeMesub({ revalidateAfter: 0 })` shows every change on the next call. A `revalidate_after` set on one answer wins, to test the cache.

sections.heading: A webhook
sections.text:
`fake.webhook` builds a delivery signed with `fake.webhookSecret`, which the fake's client verifies with:
```ts
const { body, headers } = await fake.webhook('subscription.renewed', {
    subscription: { external_id: 'user_42' },
});

await request(app)
    .post('/webhooks/mesub')
    .set(headers)
    .type('json')
    .send(body)
    .expect(200);
```
It carries the subscription the fake holds under `subscription.id` when it holds one, and a made-up one otherwise. `fake.webhook('test')` is Mesub's test delivery: `test: true`, the id `evt_test`, on its sample subscription (`sub_test`, `user_123`). Nothing is added to the fake.
`signWebhook(body, { secret })` signs a body of your own.

sections.heading: Events
Subscribing and managing
Pay now and the tier
sections.text:
`subscriptions.retry` is refused as Mesub refuses it, from what the fake holds: a parked seat (`subscription_paused`), a row not late (`subscription_not_late`), a plan past its end (`plan_ended`), and the wait between two retries (`retry_too_soon`, with `retryAfter`). The wait depends on the project's `tier`, `dev` by default:
`tier` | Retries by hand
`free` | 10 minutes apart, three per missed period (`retries_spent`), none past `retry_deadline`
`dev`, `business` | The first at once, then 20 minutes, doubling
```ts
const fake = new FakeMesub({ tier: 'free', revalidateAfter: 0 });
const late = fake.addSubscription({ wallet, plan: 'pro', status: 'unpaid' });
await fake.client().subscriptions.retry(late.id); // 202, still unpaid
await fake.client().subscriptions.retry(late.id); // retry_too_soon, retryAfter 10 minutes
```
A retry taken pulls nothing: the row stays `unpaid`. On `free`, a late row from `addSubscription` has no access; on the other tiers it keeps access through its retries. What only the chain decides (`insufficient_balance`, `retry_cannot_succeed`) or a race (`pull_running`, `subscription_changed`) is set with `fail()`, so test it on the SDK call alone, or on a route that makes that one call.

sections.heading: Over the tier's cap
sections.text:
```ts
fake.park(id); // paused, no next charge
fake.unpark(id); // charged again at the end of its period
```
This is a parked seat. Access and status stay as they are. With `accessEvents`, `park` and `unpark` raise `subscription.paused` and `subscription.unpaused`.

sections.heading: What was called
sections.text:
```ts
fake.requests; // every call: method, path, query, headers, body
```

sections.heading: With your own client

sections.text:
What each Mesub tier costs, how many plans and subscribers a project can hold, how retries differ, and the rate limits of the API.
A tier belongs to a project. Its limits count across all the plans of that project, not per plan.

sections.heading: Tiers
sections.text:
| Free | Dev | Business
Price | $0 | 20 USDC every 30 days | Custom
Plans | 1 | 3 | No limit
Subscribers | 30 | 150 | No limit
Automatic retries | None | Yes, per plan | Yes, per plan
Access while a payment is late | Off | On, until the last retry | On, until the last retry
Retries by hand | 3 per missed period | Yes | Yes
Change tier in the dashboard, under Plans.

sections.heading: What counts
sections.text:
A plan counts while it is live: pending, active, or sunset with an end date still ahead. A failed plan, or one past its end, takes no slot.
A subscriber is a wallet with a subscription that is `active`, `unpaid`, or `cancelled` and not yet past its end. A `stopped` subscription does not count: it takes a seat again only if it comes back, and only if there is room. A wallet subscribed to two of your plans counts once.
The dashboard shows both counts under Plans, in Project usage.

sections.heading: At a limit
sections.text:
At the plan limit, a new plan cannot be published.
At the subscriber limit, a new subscription is refused with `seat_cap_reached`, when it is created and again when it is submitted: of several checkouts open on the last seat, one goes through. Existing subscribers are not affected.
After a downgrade, a project can hold more subscribers than its new tier allows. The seats over the limit are parked: nothing is charged on them, and their access runs to the end of the period already paid. See parked seats.

sections.heading: API rate limits
sections.text:
Limits are per API key, per route, per minute.
Calls | Limit
Reads: `/v1/access`, `/v1/plans`, `/v1/subscriptions`, `/v1/project`, `/v1/events` | 1,000 a minute
Writes: create, transaction, submit, retry, cancel, resume, close, their confirms | 60 a minute
Requests with no key, or a wrong one, are counted by IP address: 120 a minute.
Past a limit, Mesub answers 429 `rate_limited` with a `Retry-After` header. The SDK caches access answers, so one customer checked on every request costs far fewer calls than requests.

sections.heading: Other limits
sections.text:
What | Limit
Webhook endpoints per project | 16
Subscriptions waiting for a signature, per project | 1,000
Subscriptions waiting for a signature, per customer | 5
Plans checked by one guard | 3
Retries on a plan's own policy | 10
Shortest wait between two retries | 15 minutes
A hosted MCP server that lets your AI agent read one Mesub project and act on it: what it can do, what it never can, and the risks.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.text:
An MCP server that Mesub hosts. Your AI tool connects to it, and its agent can then read one project and act on it, the way you would in the dashboard. There is nothing to install and no API key to hand over.
It is not the agent skills. The skills teach an agent to write your integration, in your codebase. The MCP server lets an agent act on your project: look at a subscription, retry a charge, add a webhook.
It is all or nothing. A connected agent can use every tool listed below. There is no read-only mode, so connect an agent only if you would let it do all of it.

sections.heading: Connect
sections.text:
1. Add the server's address to your AI tool, as a remote MCP server.
2. The tool opens a Mesub page in your browser. Sign in to the dashboard.
3. Choose one project. Nothing is chosen for you.
4. Read what the page lists, then press Authorize.
The address:
A tool configured by a JSON file takes an entry like this one:
Some tools want `"type": "http"` beside the `url`. A tool configured from a terminal takes the same two things, a name and the address. The words of the command are your tool's own, this is only its usual shape:
The page that asks you to authorize shows the name the application gave itself. Beside it is the host that publishes the application when Mesub could check one, and Unverified app when it could not. The page also says where your browser is sent back to: check both before you authorize. A request you leave open is dropped after ten minutes.
An agent works on the project you chose and no other. To work on another project, connect again and choose it.

sections.heading: What the agent can do
sections.text:
Read
Tool | What it does
`get_project` | The project, its tier, and how much of its limits is used
`list_plans` | Every plan, with its subscribers and what it collected this period. A prepared plan waits there with its link to sign
`get_plan` | One plan: its subscribers by status, its latest charges, why charges fail
`list_subscriptions` | Subscriptions, by plan or by status, or found by wallet or by your own customer id
`get_subscription` | One subscription and every charge tried on it
`check_access` | Whether a customer has access, and why not when they do not
`list_events` | What happened on a day, over the last 45 days: payments, subscribers, changes to the project. Finds a charge by wallet, your customer id or the start of its signature
`list_upcoming_charges` | The charges and retries to come, each one Mesub already expects to fail flagged with why
`get_overview` | Collected, failed and recovered over 7, 30 or 90 days
`list_webhooks` | The webhook endpoints, never their secret
`list_webhook_deliveries` | An endpoint's deliveries and what your server answered
`get_webhook_secret` | An endpoint's signing secret
`search_docs` | Search these docs. It reads nothing of your project
`ping` | Whether Mesub answers
Act
Tool | What it does
`retry_charge` | Retry a failed charge, when a customer is late. Mesub refuses one that cannot succeed or a wallet short of funds, spending no retry
`update_retry_policy` | Change how many times a plan retries, and how far apart
`create_webhook` | Add an endpoint and return its signing secret
`update_webhook` | Change the URL or the events of an endpoint, turn it off or back on
`delete_webhook` | Delete an endpoint
`regenerate_webhook_secret` | Draw a new signing secret. The old one keeps signing for `overlap_hours`, 0 to 24: at once by default
`send_test_webhook` | Send a test delivery to an endpoint
`update_project` | Rename the project
Prepare
Tool | What it does
`prepare_plan` | Fill in a plan for you. It does not exist until you sign it yourself in the dashboard
Before preparing, your agent asks you two things: whether to lock the receiving wallets (up to four, and which one is paid for now) and whether the plan ends on a date. A locked list can never change once you sign. With no list, the plan pays your own wallet.
The tools describe their own parameters to the agent, so there is nothing to learn here: ask in plain words.

sections.heading: What it can never do
sections.text:
Whatever the agent is asked, by you or by anything it reads:
- See or change your API key.
- Change the project's tier.
- Delete a project or a plan.
- Close a plan, or change the end or the receiving wallets of a plan you already signed.
- Resend an old webhook delivery.
- Read a customer's email. It can check access for an email you give it, and never gets one back: a customer is shown by wallet and by your own id.
- Cancel or change a customer's subscription. Only their wallet can.
These are not tools switched off: the server has no such tool, and Mesub gives an agent no way to them.

sections.heading: Limits
sections.text: Per connection: 120 reads and 20 changes a minute, and 5 test deliveries a minute, refused ones included. A project holds up to 10 connected agents, and an account 30 across its projects.

sections.heading: See and cut a connection
sections.text:
In the dashboard, open Developers, then Connected agents. Each line is one connection: the application, when it connected, when it was last used and when it ends.
- Revoke cuts a connection. The agent's very next call is refused.
- A connection ends by itself after a day without use. While it is used, it stays open: your tool renews its one hour token by itself.
Cutting a connection undoes nothing: what the agent changed stays as it is. To connect again, start from your tool.

sections.heading: Risks
sections.text:
A signing secret lands in your conversation. When an agent creates a webhook, regenerates its secret or reads it, the secret is in the answer, so it is in the conversation and wherever your tool keeps it. Move it to your server's environment, and regenerate it if the conversation is shared.
What the agent reads is written by other people. A plan's name, what a webhook endpoint answered, the identifier of a customer: all of it is text somebody else chose, and it can be written to look like an instruction. The server tells every agent to treat it as data. An agent can still be steered by it. That is why the tools that move money or break an integration, such as retrying a charge, deleting a webhook or regenerating its secret, are marked so that your tool asks you first. Keep that question on, and read it.
You review every prepared plan. The agent fills it in, you sign it. Read the price, the token, the period, the end and above all the receiving wallets in the dashboard before you do: each one is shown in full and marked when it is not on your account. You can still edit the plan there first.

- "Why does this customer have no access?"
- "Which renewals are at risk this week?"
- "Add a webhook for failed payments and give me the secret for my .env"

For what the answers mean, see the lifecycle and check access.

A kit of skills that teach an AI coding agent to write your Mesub integration in your codebase, whichever agent you use: install it, what each skill covers, how to ask, and what it never does.
A skill is a folder of instructions that an AI coding agent reads when a task calls for it. The Mesub kit holds seven of them. With the kit installed, an agent asked to add subscriptions to your app follows Mesub's own steps and rules instead of guessing:
- your API key stays on your server;
- access is checked on your server, not by hiding a button;
- who is asking comes from your own login, never from the request.
The kit is one set of folders in the open Agent Skills format. It is the same for every agent that reads that format.
The skills are experimental: they work today and can change without notice, so read what your agent writes as you would any pull request.

sections.heading: Install
sections.text:
From the root of your project, with the skills CLI:
```bash
# See what the kit holds, without installing
npx skills add Mesub-io/skills --list

# Pick skills and agents interactively
npx skills add Mesub-io/skills

# Every skill of the kit, no prompt
npx skills add Mesub-io/skills --skill '*' --yes

# One skill, no prompt
npx skills add Mesub-io/skills --skill mesub-quickstart --yes
```
Each skill lands in `.agents/skills/<skill>/` of your project, and the CLI links it for an agent that reads another folder. Add `-g` to install in your user folder instead. It also writes `skills-lock.json`, which records what was installed. Commit both if your team should share them.
Each skill works alone, so you can take one without the others. An install copies the skill's folder and nothing else.
Without the CLI, a skill is a folder to copy into the place your agent reads skills from:
```bash
git clone --depth 1 https://github.com/Mesub-io/skills.git mesub-skills
cp -R mesub-skills/skills/<skill> <your agent's skills folder>/
```
To update, run `npx skills update`. It fetches the skills again from the repository.
The skills wire `@mesub/node` and `@mesub/react`, both on npm. An agent that has the kit checks what is installed first, and when a package is missing it stops and tells you: it does not install a package with a similar name or rewrite the calls by hand.

sections.heading: The skills
sections.text:
There is nothing to call: your agent picks a skill up by itself when the task matches.
Skill | The agent uses it when
`mesub-quickstart` | Your project has no Mesub code yet: from nothing to a first subscriber, on Express, Next.js or NestJS
`mesub-gate-access` | A route or a page is for the subscribers of a plan: checking access and answering a refusal correctly
`mesub-subscribe-and-manage` | Users subscribe, cancel, resume or close, with the React widget or from your server (subscribe, manage)
`mesub-webhooks` | Your server receives Mesub's events: the signature, duplicates, retries
`mesub-testing` | Tests must cover your integration without calling Mesub or touching the chain
`mesub-errors` | A call, a route or a payment fails, and the cause must be found from an error code or a reason
`mesub-mcp` | It is connected to the MCP server and acts on your live project: read it, find why a payment failed, manage webhooks, prepare a plan
`mesub-quickstart` also carries the directory of the kit: start there if you install only one.

sections.heading: How to ask
sections.text:
In plain words. You do not have to name a skill, or Mesub's vocabulary:
- "Add Mesub to this app and gate the dashboard on the pro plan"
- "Add a cancel button to the account page"
- "Handle the failed payment webhook"
- "Write tests for the access check"
- "Subscribing throws a 409, find out why"
The agent will ask you for what it cannot know: the plan's slug, and to put `MESUB_API_KEY` in your server's environment yourself.

sections.heading: What the skills never do
sections.text:
Every skill tells the agent not to:
- Ask for your API key in the conversation, or read its value. It checks that the name is set, nothing more.
- Write the key in code, in a log, or in a variable your bundler ships to the browser.
- Take the customer from the request: a query, a body, a header. It comes from the session your app verified.
- Install a lookalike when a package is missing.
- Say the integration is tested end to end. A subscription needs a person with a wallet, so the agent reports what it checked and what is left for you to click.
The scripts a skill ships only read your project: no write, no install, no outbound call, and they never print a key.
These are instructions, not a lock. An agent can still get one wrong, which is one more reason to read the diff.

sections.heading: Skills and the MCP server
sections.text: The skills teach an agent to write your integration, in your codebase. The MCP server lets an agent act on your project: look at a subscription, retry a charge. One does not need the other.

sections.heading: Source and problems
sections.text:
The kit is public, under Apache-2.0: github.com/Mesub-io/skills. Each skill is plain text, so you can read what your agent will be told before you install it.
If a skill made your agent write something wrong, or missed a case, open an issue with what you asked and what it wrote. Leave your API key out of it.

The base URL of the Mesub API, how a request is authenticated, the conventions every route follows, and the list of routes with their SDK call.
`@mesub/node` wraps this API. Use it directly from any other language.

sections.heading: Base URL
sections.text:
```bash
curl "https://api.mesub.io/v1/project" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MESUB_API_KEY"
```
Every route lives under `https://api.mesub.io/v1` and takes the project's API key as a bearer token. The key identifies the project: there is no project id in any path. Authentication has the detail.

sections.heading: Conventions
sections.text:
- Fields are in snake case.
- Dates are ISO 8601 strings in UTC.
- Token amounts are strings in the token's smallest unit: `"9990000"` is 9.99 of a token with six decimals.
- Statuses and reasons are lowercase. Mesub may add one later: keep a default branch.
- A field the route does not know is refused with a 400, not ignored.
- Every error has the same body, with a `code` to branch on.

sections.heading: API version
sections.text:
The contract of `/v1` is versioned by date. Name the version you wrote your code against in the `Mesub-Version` header:
```bash
curl "https://api.mesub.io/v1/project" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MESUB_API_KEY" \
  -H "Mesub-Version: 2026-10-02"
```
`2026-10-02` is the only version served today, and no answer depends on the version yet. `@mesub/node` sends the header on every call.
You send | Mesub answers
A version Mesub serves | As that version
No header | As the first version, `2026-10-02`
Anything else, an empty header too | 400 `unsupported_version`
The message of an `unsupported_version` lists the versions served. The API key is checked first: a missing or wrong key answers 401 whatever the header says.
Every answer, errors included, says the version it was served as in its own `Mesub-Version` header.

sections.heading: Try a request
sections.text:
Each route's page has a Try it button. It opens a panel where you paste an API key, fill the parameters and send the request from your browser.
Calls are real: they act on the project the key belongs to. The key stays in your browser and goes only to the API.
The whole API is also described in one OpenAPI file, which these pages are drawn from. It was copied from .
