sections.heading: Pagination
sections.text:
Lists take `limit` (1 to 100, 20 by default, 25 on events) and `starting_after`, the id of the last item of the previous page, and answer `{ data, has_more }`. Items come newest first.
```bash
curl -G "https://api.mesub.io/v1/subscriptions" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MESUB_API_KEY" \
  -d external_id=user_42 \
  -d limit=50 \
  -d starting_after=cmg1x0abc0001
```
With the SDK, `subscriptions.listAll` and `subscriptions.allAttempts` walk every page for you.

sections.heading: Webhooks
sections.text: Mesub also calls you. Webhooks lists every event and its payload.

Send the project's API key as a bearer token on every request. What a missing or wrong key answers, and how many calls a key may make.
Every request carries the project's API key in the `Authorization` header, as a bearer token:
```bash
curl "https://api.mesub.io/v1/project" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MESUB_API_KEY"
```
A project has one key at a time, and the key is the project: every route answers about that project only, and no call names a project id. The key starts with `SUB_`. Get your API key says where to create it and how to rotate it.
The key goes in the header, never in the query string: a query string ends up in access logs and in browser history.
Keep the key on your server. It creates subscriptions and reads your subscribers, so it never goes in a browser, a mobile app or a repository.

sections.heading: When the key is refused
sections.text:
Status | `code` | Meaning
401 | `missing_api_key` | No `Authorization: Bearer` header was sent
401 | `invalid_api_key` | Not a key Mesub issued, or one rotated since
```json
{
    "statusCode": 401,
    "message": "That API key is not valid.",
    "error": "Unauthorized",
    "code": "invalid_api_key",
    "retryable": false
}
```

sections.heading: Rate limits
sections.text:
Limits are per API key, per route, per minute.
Calls | Limit
Reads: `/v1/access`, `/v1/plans`, `/v1/subscriptions`, `/v1/project`, `/v1/events` | 1,000 a minute
Writes: create, transaction, submit, retry, cancel, resume, close, their confirms | 60 a minute
Requests with no key, or with a wrong one, are counted by IP address instead: 120 a minute.
Past a limit, Mesub answers 429 `rate_limited` with a `Retry-After` header. Pricing and limits has every other limit.

The body every error of the Mesub API carries, how to branch on its code, when to retry, and the full list of error codes with their status.
Every error has the same body:
```json
{
    "statusCode": 409,
    "message": "You are already subscribed to this plan.",
    "error": "Conflict",
    "code": "already_subscribed",
    "retryable": false,
    "request_id": "req_4f8KzQ2nVb7XcR1mT9wLp3sD"
}
```
Field | What it says
`statusCode` | The HTTP status, repeated
`message` | A sentence for a person. A validation error answers a list of them. It may be reworded
`error` | The status's name
`code` | What your code reads
`retryable` | Whether the same request, sent again unchanged, may succeed later
`request_id` | The request's id, as the `Mesub-Request-Id` header says it. Quote it to Mesub support
Branch on `code`, never on `message`. A code is never moved to another status or reused, and is renamed only in a new `Mesub-Version`, but new ones are added: keep a default branch.
One exception was made before the first integrator, within `2026-10-02`: `plan_deleted` became `plan_removed`, and `plan_rebuilt` became `plan_replaced`. The old names are no longer answered. Code written against them must branch on the new ones.
When `retryable` is true, the same request sent again unchanged may succeed later; a `Retry-After` header says when, in seconds. It never means "retry at once". Every route is safe to call twice.
Each route's page lists the codes that route answers. This page lists them all.

sections.text:
`201`: The subscription as it now stands: `active` when it landed. With a `reason` and its `reason_code`, nothing was settled: still `pending` when nothing landed, `failed` when what landed is not what Mesub built. The codes this route answers today: `transaction_failed`, `transaction_expired`, `nothing_landed`, `subscription_mismatch`, `subscription_remade`, `earlier_subscription_running`, `not_our_transaction`, `dev_not_running`.
`subscription`: One subscription to one of your project's plans.
`reason`: Present only when nothing was settled, or when what landed is not what Mesub built, and always with `reason_code`. A sentence for a person, which Mesub may reword: branch on `reason_code`, never on this.
`reason_code`: Why, for a program: present exactly when `reason` is. Stable and in snake case, never reworded. An open family rather than a closed list: Mesub adds codes without a new version, so keep a default branch. Known today: - `not_our_transaction`: the signature is not of a transaction Mesub co-signed over terms the wallet signed for this subscription. - `transaction_failed`: the transaction landed and the chain refused it: nothing it held happened. - `transaction_expired`: its blockhash ran out before it landed: it never will. - `nothing_landed`: on a submit, no subscription stands at its address yet: it stays `pending`. - `subscription_not_on_chain`: on a cancel or a resume, the subscription no longer exists on chain. - `subscription_mismatch`: what landed names another wallet, plan, amount or billing period than the subscription reserved, which is now `failed`. - `dev_not_running`: Mesub's own Dev plan landed cancelled or part paid, and is now `failed`. - `earlier_subscription_running`: a comeback paid while the subscription it came back over ran again: Mesub was told and sorts it out. - `subscription_remade`: on a submit, it landed, and the subscription was closed and made again without Mesub since: now `failed`. - `cancellation_not_landed`: the subscription stands on chain with no cancellation. - `resume_not_landed`: the subscription stands on chain still cancelled. - `close_not_landed`: the subscription still stands on chain. - `subscription_changed`: the subscription moved on while the cancellation was read, and was left as it is. - `subscription_not_cancelled`: on a resume, the subscription is no longer cancelled: nothing to resume. - `cancelled_subscription_remade`: on a resume, the subscription cancelled was closed and made again without Mesub since: it stays `cancelled`. - `resume_unverified`: on a resume, the subscription on chain cannot be told to be the one cancelled: it stays `cancelled`.

`api_version`: The version of this contract `data` and `detail` are written in, as `Mesub-Version` names them. Set when the body is written, and kept with it. One of `2026-10-02`.

Mesub posts an event to your endpoints when a subscription changes. This section is the reference of what is sent. To set an endpoint up and write its handler, read the Webhooks guide.

sections.heading: The request
sections.text:
Each delivery is a `POST` to your endpoint, with a JSON body and three headers:
Header | What it holds
`webhook-id` | The delivery's id: one per event and per endpoint, the same on every retry
`webhook-timestamp` | When this attempt was sent, in Unix seconds
`webhook-signature` | `v1,` then the signature of this attempt, in base64. Sometimes two, see below
Deliveries are signed the Standard Webhooks way: an HMAC-SHA256 of `webhook-id.webhook-timestamp.body`, keyed with the endpoint's signing secret, the part after `whsec_` decoded from base64. The signature covers the exact bytes sent, so verify the raw body.
When you regenerate a secret with an overlap, the old secret keeps signing beside the new one until the overlap ends. Every attempt in that window carries two signatures, space separated, the new secret's first:
```text
webhook-signature: v1,<signed with the new secret> v1,<signed with the old secret>
```
Check each `v1,` signature, and accept the delivery when any one matches. `mesub.webhooks.verify` does both for you.

    "network": "mainnet-beta",

`object` | Always `event`
`type` | The event's name
`created_at` | When Mesub wrote the event. On an access event, or a cancellation's end, `detail.changed_at` is the moment

sections.heading: Ends, parked seats
sections.text:
`ended` at a cancellation's expiry, `paused` and `unpaused` are not sent yet: like the access events, they are off until Mesub turns them on. `ended` on a close is sent today.

A cancellation reaches its expiry | `subscription.ended`, `end_reason: "cancelled"`, usually within 30 min

sections.heading: Access events
sections.text:
`subscription.access_granted` and `subscription.access_revoked` are sent when the access a subscription grants actually changes, and only then. Every change sends one, whatever made it: a payment, a cancellation reaching its end, a plan's end date, a blocked charge reaching `access_until`. A renewal paid on time, or a resume while the paid period runs, changes nothing and sends neither.
Mesub does not send them yet: they are off until Mesub turns them on. Until then, read access with `GET /v1/access`.

`data.blocked_since` | Since when charges are held for a cause not the customer's, or null
`data.blocked_reason` | Why they are held, or null
`detail.changed_at` | When access changed, to the millisecond: the moment `data` describes
`detail.blocked_reason` | Why charges were held when access changed, or null

`created_at` is when Mesub wrote the event, and can come later than `detail.changed_at`: a date that passed with nothing else happening is told a few seconds after it.
`detail.blocked_reason` and `detail.access_until` describe the change itself. Drive your customer's access from these two events alone; the others say why it changed. An event without `sequence` cannot be placed: read the subscription's state now, with Retrieve a subscription or Check access, rather than applying its `data`.
`data`: The subscription as it stood right after the change that raised this event, as Retrieve a subscription would have answered it then, however late the delivery. Events raised by the same change share it, and `detail` says what each event is about: a last retry that fails raises `subscription.payment_failed` and `subscription.stopped`, both showing `status: stopped`, the failure's cause in `payment_failed`'s `detail`.
`detail`: The event's own fields.
`detail.changed_at`: When access actually changed: the moment `data` describes. A date that passed with nothing else happening (the end of a paid period, of a cancellation, of the plan) is that date to the millisecond, even when Mesub wrote the event later. Keep, per subscription, the latest `changed_at` you applied, and the access it set.
`detail.blocked_reason`: Why the subscription's charges were held when access changed, in the words of `data.blocked_reason`. Null when they were not. Mesub may add a value: keep a default branch. Absent on an event written before Mesub added it. One of `puller_not_allowed`, `receiver_not_allowed`, `receiver_account_missing`, `receiver_account_frozen`, `mint_gone`, `mesub`.
`detail.access_until`: The date access ended: the end of a paid period, of a cancellation, of the plan, or of the access a held subscription keeps (`blocked_reason`). Never after `changed_at`. Null when access ended with no date of its own, a stop for example. Absent on an event written before Mesub added it.
`test`: True on a test delivery of this event, sent by hand from the dashboard. Absent otherwise.

sections.heading: Headers
sections.text:
`webhook-id`: The delivery's id: one per event and per endpoint, the same on every retry of that delivery and on a resend from the dashboard. Deduplicate on it. Two endpoints receiving one event get two ids.
`webhook-timestamp`: When this attempt was sent, in Unix seconds: new on every retry, and signed with the body. Refuse one too far from your own clock.
`webhook-signature`: `v1,` then the base64 HMAC-SHA256 of `webhook-id.webhook-timestamp.body`, keyed with the endpoint's signing secret (the part after `whsec_`, base64 decoded), the Standard Webhooks way. It may hold several, space separated: two while a regenerated secret's overlap runs, the new secret's first. Accept the delivery when any one matches your secret. Check it over the raw bytes received, before parsing them.
